docs.title: MoE Models from Scratch
docs.text:
A LaTeX-first technical book that builds a Mixture-of-Experts language model — MiniDeepSeekMoE-16x2 — from scratch in PyTorch, one runnable section at a time.

Every chapter is the same shape:

problem opening → visual anchor → tensor / math mechanics → implementation listing → falsifiable diagnostic → bridge

Each section ships a .tex file (the production source), a co-located .md (this site), four standalone artifact wrappers (figure, table, listing, equation), and a runnable Python module + example script + pytest under src/, examples/, tests/.

docs.title: The build ladder
docs.text:
1. From dense compute to conditional compute — why the dense FFN is the bottleneck and what MoE actually replaces. (complete)
  2. A dense Transformer baseline from scratch — embeddings, attention, dense FFN, training loop.
  3. Experts, routers, and the first MoE layer — the naive routed FFN.
  4. Top-1 routing and Switch-style dispatch — assignment masks, capacity, dropped tokens.
  5. Top-2 routing and weighted expert combination — normalized gates, the routing story made vectorized.
  6. Vectorized dispatch, capacity, and routing efficiency — flattened batches, equivalence tests against the naive layer.
  7. Router training and load-balancing losses — auxiliary loss, z-loss, routing dashboards.
  8. Shared experts and fine-grained routed experts — the DeepSeekMoE-style expert structure.
  9. Auxiliary-loss-free load balancing — the router-bias mechanism: biased selection, unbiased combine.
  10. Assembling MiniDeepSeekMoE end to end — config object, full forward pass, training and sampling scripts.
  11. Training, diagnostics, and controlled experiments — ablation matrix, loss curves, expert behaviour.
  12. Inference, performance, and scaling beyond the toy model — active-parameter accounting, expert parallelism.

docs.title: The invariant the whole book protects
docs.text:
router bias affects expert selection only;
final combine weights are computed from unbiased selected scores.

The decoder interface stays \((B, T, D) \to (B, T, D)\) at every step of the ladder.

docs.title: 1.1 The dense FFN bottleneck
docs.text:
A dense decoder layer has a sub-layer that almost every paper draws as a small unmarked box: the feed-forward network. It is a two-matrix block that lifts each token from width \(D\) to a wider hidden space \(H\) and projects it back. Once you count what that block actually does, it is the most expensive part of the layer, and it is the part that has nothing to do with the token's identity. Self-attention reuses information across positions. The dense FFN, by contrast, runs the same heavy computation for every token independently. That is the cost we want to make visible before we propose any sparsity.

Figure 1.1 — Dense decoder block with the FFN path highlighted as the always-on compute region. Self-attention is drawn in muted gray and the FFN in saturated purple precisely because that is where the always-on compute lives. Rendered via TikZ in the PDF version.

tokens (B,T,D) ──► self-attention ──► [ Dense FFN: W1 (D×H), W2 (H×D) ] ──► output (B,T,D)
                                       ▲
                                       every token → all H hidden units
                                       cost per token = 2·D·H MADs

Fix the smallest example that still has the bottleneck in it. Take a four-token batch with \(D = 8\) and an FFN expansion factor of \(4\), so \(H = 32\). Each token enters the FFN as a length-\(8\) vector and walks through a \(D \times H = 8 \times 32\) matrix, becomes a length-\(32\) activation, and walks back through an \(H \times D = 32 \times 8\) matrix. Count the multiply-adds along that walk and you are counting how much compute the layer charges this batch.

Before writing the cost down, name the tensors. Let \(B\) be the batch size, \(T\) the sequence length, \(D\) the model width, and \(H\) the FFN hidden width. Flatten the batch and the sequence into a single token axis of length \(N = B\,T\), so the block sees a token matrix of shape \((N, D)\). The up-projection \(W_1\) has shape \((D, H)\) and the down-projection \(W_2\) has shape \((H, D)\). The hidden activation is \(h = \mathrm{GELU}(x W_1) \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times H}\); the output is \(y = h W_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}\). Everything stays in the decoder's \((B, T, D)\) interface, which is the invariant we promised to keep all the way to the end of the build ladder.

Table 1.1 — Shape and cost contract for the dense FFN block. Every token traverses every hidden unit, so cost scales with the product \(N \cdot D \cdot H\).

Concept Local definition Shape / code object Why it matters / check Block input \(x\) Hidden state arriving at the FFN sub-layer of a decoder block. \((B, T, D)\); x: Tensor Decoder interface stays \(x \to y\) with shape \((B,T,D)\). Up-projection \(W_1\) Maps each token from width \(D\) to the wider hidden space \(H\). \((D, H)\); DenseFFN.up.weight Cost grows linearly in \(H\): increase \(H\) and every token pays more. Hidden activation \(h\) The expanded representation \(h = \mathrm{GELU}(x W_1)\). \((B, T, H)\); F.gelu(self.up(x)) Materialised for every token, even when most coordinates are tiny. Down-projection \(W_2\) Projects \(h\) back to model width. \((H, D)\); DenseFFN.down.weight Doubles the per-token MAD count; symmetric partner of \(W_1\). Per-token cost MADs paid by one token to traverse \(W_1\) then \(W_2\). \(2 D H\); cost.mads_per_token Falsifiable: dense_ffn_cost reports \(512\) for \(D=8, H=32\). Failure mode Treating \(H\) as "free" because parameters look small. — Doubling \(H\) doubles compute for every token in the batch.

The accounting is now mechanical. The up-projection costs \(N D H\) multiply-adds (one for every entry of an \(N \times H\) output, each accumulating \(D\) products). The down-projection costs the symmetric \(N H D\). Their sum is the cost of the block.

\[ \mathrm{MADs}_{\text{dense FFN}}(N, D, H) \;=\; \underbrace{N \cdot D \cdot H}_{\text{up-projection } x W_1} \;+\; \underbrace{N \cdot H \cdot D}_{\text{down-projection } h W_2} \;=\; 2 \, N \, D \, H . \]

Two things in the equation matter. First, the cost is the product of three independent knobs: the token count \(N\), the model width \(D\), and the hidden width \(H\). Touching any of them moves cost linearly. Second, the cost has no token-specific term. There is no \(i\) in the expression, no notion of "which token is this". The block charges the same compute for a punctuation token as for a high-information word.

We can turn this into a tiny piece of runnable code that we will rely on across the book whenever we need to compare a dense baseline against a routed alternative. The function below mirrors the cost formula one-for-one; the matching PyTorch DenseFFN module lives next to it under src/moe_from_scratch/ch01/ and is the block we will literally replace in Chapter 3.

def dense_ffn_cost(n_tokens, d_model, hidden):
    # W1: (D, H) and W2: (H, D); biases ignored.
    params         = 2 * d_model * hidden          # storage
    mads_per_token = 2 * d_model * hidden          # x @ W1  +  h @ W2
    total_mads     = n_tokens * mads_per_token     # linear in N and in H
    return params, mads_per_token, total_mads

# Mini-example: a 4-token batch, d_model = 8, FFN expansion factor 4 (so H = 32).
params, per_tok, total = dense_ffn_cost(n_tokens=4, d_model=8, hidden=32)
assert (params, per_tok, total) == (512, 512, 2048)

The assert is the section's falsifiable check: for the mini-example, the block stores \(512\) parameters, spends \(512\) multiply-adds per token, and \(2048\) multiply-adds in total. Break the cost formula — swap \(2 D H\) for \(D H\), say, or forget the down-projection — and the assertion fails. The companion script under examples/ch01/ repeats the mini-example, then sweeps \(H \in \{16, 32, 64, 128, 256\}\) and prints a small table; the total MAD column strictly increases, with each doubling of \(H\) doubling the total. That is the bottleneck made explicit: the dense FFN's cost goes up linearly with \(H\), and every token in the batch pays the same multiplier.

Diagnostic. A small cost table proving that increasing \(H\) increases every token path. Run python examples/ch01/section_1_1_dense_ffn_cost.py and verify that the printed MAD totals satisfy \(1024 < 2048 < 4096 < 8192 < 16384\) for \(H \in \{16, 32, 64, 128, 256\}\), and that pytest tests/ch01/ -q reports 11 passing tests.

Once the bottleneck is visible, the next question is whether every token really needs the same FFN.

docs.title: 1.2 Conditional compute as the central idea
docs.text:
Section 1.1 ended on an uncomfortable number: every token in the batch pays \(2 D H\) multiply-adds, and the only way to make the FFN "smarter" was to push \(H\) up and pay more. Conditional compute attacks that constraint directly. Instead of one fixed FFN, place a bank of \(E\) small FFNs inside the layer and choose, per token, which \(K\) of them to run. The model now has many more parameters than before, but any individual token still pays for only \(K\) of those experts. MoE is not a new model family — it is a selective FFN.

Figure 1.2 — Conditional compute schematic. Four tokens flow through a router that emits a score vector of length \(E\); only the top-\(K\) experts per token (drawn as solid green routes) run their FFN. The expert bank grows with \(E\), but every token still pays only for \(K\) experts. Rendered via TikZ in the PDF version.

t1 ─┐                              ┌── expert 1 ──┐
t2 ─┤    ┌─────────────────────┐   ├── expert 2 ──┤
t3 ─┼───►│ router: scores (N,E)│──►├── expert 3 ──┼──► output (B,T,D)
t4 ─┘    └─────────────────────┘   └── expert 4 ──┘
              top-K = 2 per token        bank of E = 4 experts
              active fraction α = K / E = 0.5

Figure 1.2 shows the picture in one frame: tokens enter, the router emits a score row per token, the top-\(K\) routes are highlighted in green, and the unchosen routes stay muted. Take the same mini-example we used to measure the dense block (\(N = 4\) tokens, \(D = 8\), \(H = 32\)) and replace its single FFN with a bank of \(E = 4\) experts. Each expert is a dense FFN of exactly the shape we already counted: \(2 D H = 512\) parameters. Pick \(K = 2\) experts per token and you have run two dense FFNs for each of the four tokens. Compare that against making the bank bigger (\(E = 16\), \(K = 2\) unchanged) and a useful asymmetry appears: the bank quadruples, but each token's compute does not move.

Three numbers carry this section. The token count \(N = B\,T\) and the FFN shape constants \(D\) and \(H\) are inherited from Section 1.1. The two new constants are \(E\), the number of experts in the bank, and \(K\), the number of experts each token activates. The router's output is a tensor of shape \((N, E)\) of real-valued scores; selecting the top-\(K\) entries per row produces an index tensor of shape \((N, K)\) that names which experts run for each token. The decoder interface \((B, T, D) \to (B, T, D)\) is untouched.

Table 1.2 — Dense baseline versus conditional-compute MoE for \(N=4\) tokens, \(D=8\), \(H=32\). Growing the expert bank \(E\) inflates total parameters but leaves per-token compute pinned to \(K \cdot 2 D H\).

Quantity Dense baseline MoE path Caveat Measurement Total FFN parameters \(P_{\text{bank}}\) \(2 D H = 512\) \(E \cdot 2 D H\): grows with the expert count (\(E{=}4 \to 2048\); \(E{=}16 \to 8192\)) MoE does not reduce parameters. It enlarges the bank. cost.bank_params Activated params / token \(P^{\text{token}}_{\text{active}}\) \(2 D H = 512\) \(K \cdot 2 D H\): depends on \(K\) only; \(K{=}2 \to 1024\) Equal to running \(K\) dense FFNs for that token. cost.active_params_per_token Active fraction \(\alpha\) \(1.0\) \(K / E\) (\(\tfrac{2}{4}=0.5\) or \(\tfrac{2}{16}=0.125\)) Shrinks as you scale \(E\); the bank gets sparser, not the compute per token. cost.active_fraction Per-batch active MADs \(N \cdot 2 D H = 2048\) \(N \cdot K \cdot 2 D H = 4096\) Compute per token is fixed; the bank size \(E\) has no effect on this column. cost.active_mads Failure mode — Confusing \(\alpha\) shrink with a wall-clock speedup. Reduced activated compute is not automatic wall-clock speedup; dispatch overhead lives in later chapters. Watch FLOPs vs runtime in Ch.11/12

The accounting follows from the picture. The expert bank stores \(E\) copies of the dense FFN, so its parameter count is \(E\) times the dense number. For any one token, only \(K\) of those experts contribute compute, so the activated parameter count per token is \(K\) times the dense number. The ratio of these two quantities is the section's headline number, the active fraction \(\alpha = K/E\).

\[ \underbrace{P_{\text{bank}} = E \cdot (2 D H)}_{\text{total expert parameters}} \qquad \underbrace{P_{\text{active}}^{\text{token}} = K \cdot (2 D H)}_{\text{activated per token}} \qquad \underbrace{\alpha = \tfrac{K}{E}}_{\text{active fraction}} . \]

The equation is deliberately small because the trade it encodes is the central one. The total parameter bank \(P_{\text{bank}}\) grows linearly in \(E\); the activated parameters per token \(P^{\text{token}}_{\text{active}}\) grow linearly in \(K\). Set \(K\) small and \(E\) large and \(\alpha\) shrinks: the bank gets sparser, not the per-token compute. Notice what the equation does not promise. It does not promise wall-clock speedup — that depends on dispatch and is the subject of Chapters 6 and 12. It does not promise fewer total parameters — \(E\) multiplies them. It promises one thing: per-token compute is decoupled from total parameter count.

The cost formula has a one-line code analogue, and the smallest possible router output is one line of PyTorch. Both fragments below are in src/moe_from_scratch/ch01/conditional_compute.py as expert_bank_cost and topk_expert_ids; the example script under examples/ch01/ drives them with the mini-example.

def expert_bank_cost(n_tokens, d_model, hidden, n_experts, top_k):
    expert_params           = 2 * d_model * hidden        # one dense FFN
    bank_params             = n_experts * expert_params   # E experts in the bank
    active_params_per_token = top_k * expert_params       # only K run per token
    active_fraction         = top_k / n_experts           # K / E
    active_mads             = n_tokens * top_k * expert_params
    return bank_params, active_params_per_token, active_fraction, active_mads

# Smallest possible "router output": top-k expert IDs per token.
def topk_expert_ids(scores, top_k):
    # scores: (N, E) real numbers; one row per token, one column per expert.
    _, indices = torch.topk(scores, k=top_k, dim=-1)
    return indices                                         # (N, K) long

# Mini-example: E = 4, K = 2 vs. E = 16, K = 2, with N = 4, D = 8, H = 32.
small = expert_bank_cost(4, 8, 32, n_experts=4,  top_k=2)
big   = expert_bank_cost(4, 8, 32, n_experts=16, top_k=2)
assert small[2] == 0.5   and small[3] == 4096   # K/E = 1/2, 4096 active MADs
assert big[2]   == 0.125 and big[3]   == 4096   # K/E = 1/8, same active MADs

The two asserts are the section's falsifiable check. With \(E = 4\), \(K = 2\), the active fraction is \(0.5\); with \(E = 16\), \(K = 2\), it is \(0.125\); and in both cases the activated MAD total is \(4096\). Break the link between \(\alpha\) and \(K/E\) — replace top_k / n_experts with top_k / n_tokens, say — and the assertion fails immediately. The companion script prints both rows side by side, then samples random scores and routes the four tokens through topk_expert_ids so the reader sees that "the router" is, at this stage of the book, two lines of PyTorch returning a \((N, K)\) index tensor.

Diagnostic. Compute the active fraction for \(E = 4,\,K = 2\) and \(E = 16,\,K = 2\). Run python examples/ch01/section_1_2_conditional_compute.py and verify \(\alpha = 0.5\) in the first row, \(\alpha = 0.125\) in the second, and active_mads identical at \(4096\) in both. Then run pytest tests/ch01/ -q and expect at least 14 additional tests covering the cost formulas and the top-\(K\) chooser.

Selective compute creates a new component: the router, which needs its own tensor contract.

docs.title: 1.3 A tiny routing story
docs.text:
Section 1.2 ended with a slogan — run \(K\) of \(E\) experts per token — but the slogan did not say what data flows between the router, the experts, and the combine. Before we open any model code, walk one batch through that picture by hand. Use four tokens, four experts, and the smallest non-trivial setting, top-\(K = 2\). Every number in this section is materialised; the section's contract is the resulting set of tensor shapes.

Figure 1.3 — A storyboard of one MoE layer step: the four tokens {cat, sat, code, runs} produce a \((4,4)\) router-score matrix; the two highest scores per row (green) are selected; their softmax values become the gate matrix (gold, rows sum to 1); the gates weight the selected expert outputs to form \(y_t\). Rendered via TikZ in the PDF version.

tokens                scores (N,E)              top-K picks                gates (N,K)            output
                  ┌─────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────┐     ┌──────────┐
cat   ─► │ 2.0  0.3  1.5 -1.0 │ ─► │ ●            ● │ ─► │ 0.62  0.38 │
sat   ─► │ 0.5  2.5  0.2  1.0 │ ─► │     ●         ● │ ─► │ 0.82  0.18 │ ─► y = Σ g · expert
code  ─► │-0.5  1.2  2.0  0.8 │ ─► │     ●  ●       │ ─► │ 0.69  0.31 │
runs  ─► │ 0.1  0.7  0.4  1.9 │ ─► │     ●         ● │ ─► │ 0.77  0.23 │
                  └─────────────────┘     └─────────────────┘     └──────────┘
                                              K = 2 per row              rows sum to 1

Pick four words: [cat, sat, code, runs]. They are stand-ins, so we will not embed them; instead we hand-code a \((4, 4)\) router-score matrix that says how much each word "wants" each expert. The dense FFN of Section 1.1 had no such matrix: every token went through the same block. The MoE layer needs one, and Figure 1.3 shows where it sits in the data flow.

Name the tensors before we start writing them. Let \(N\) be the flattened token count and \(E\) the expert count (here \(N = E = 4\)). The router emits a score tensor \(s \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times E}\) with \(s_{t,i}\) the score of token \(t\) for expert \(i\). Apply \(\operatorname{top}{-}K\) over the last axis to get a selection \(\mathcal{T}_t \subset \{1, \dots, E\}\) of size \(K = 2\) per token; that gives an index tensor of shape \((N, K)\) and a values tensor of the same shape. Run softmax over only the selected values (not all \(E\)) and you have a gate tensor \(g \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times K}\) whose rows sum to one. The combine \(y_t = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}_t} g_{t,i} \, \mathrm{expert}_i(x_t)\) then produces an output of shape \((N, D)\). The decoder interface \((B, T, D)\) is intact.

Table 1.3 — Tensor contract for one MoE layer step. The toy story instantiates this with \(N=4\), \(E=4\), \(K=2\), and hand-coded scores.

Concept Local definition Shape / code object Why it matters / check Router scores \(s\) Real-valued affinity of token \(t\) for expert \(i\). \((N, E)\); story.scores Whatever produces these, the rest of the layer treats them as opaque. Top-\(K\) index set \(\mathcal{T}_t\) Indices of the \(K\) largest entries of row \(s_t\). \((N, K)\); story.indices from torch.topk Selects which experts run; everything outside \(\mathcal{T}_t\) is dropped. Selected scores Values of \(s_{t,i}\) at \(i \in \mathcal{T}_t\), in descending order. \((N, K)\); first return of torch.topk Input to the gate softmax; sorted so gate[0] is the largest. Gates \(g_{t,i}\) Softmax over selected scores, \(i \in \mathcal{T}_t\). \((N, K)\); story.gates Falsifiable: \(\sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}_t} g_{t,i} = 1\) for every token. Expert output \(\mathrm{expert}_i(x_t)\) What expert \(i\) would emit if it ran on token \(t\). \((D,)\) per call; later \((N, D)\) when batched Only \(K\) of these are computed per token; the rest are skipped. Combined output \(y_t\) Weighted combine \(\sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}_t} g_{t,i} \, \mathrm{expert}_i(x_t)\). \((N, D)\); story.combined Reads out the gate matrix into the chosen columns when experts are one-hot. Failure mode Softmax taken over all \(E\) scores before top-\(K\). — Gates would no longer sum to 1 on the selected \(K\) alone; the diagnostic catches this.

The equation is the only thing the rest of the book needs to remember from this section.

\[ \mathcal{T}_t = \operatorname*{top\,K}_{i \in \{1,\dots,E\}} s_{t,i}, \qquad g_{t,i} = \frac{\exp(s_{t,i})}{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{T}_t} \exp(s_{t,j})} \;\;\text{for}\;\; i \in \mathcal{T}_t, \qquad y_t = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}_t} g_{t,i} \, \mathrm{expert}_i(x_t) . \]

The equation has three steps in one line. The first picks indices; nothing has been weighted yet. The second normalises the \(K\) selected scores into a per-token probability distribution; the unselected \(E - K\) experts contribute zero. The third combines the chosen experts' outputs with those weights. The crucial detail is that the softmax is taken after top-\(K\), only over the selected entries. Taking the softmax first and then sub-selecting would leave the gates summing to something less than one, which is the failure mode the table calls out.

The listing below realises the equation as a handful of lines of PyTorch and matches src/moe_from_scratch/ch01/routing_story.py. The experts are kept deliberately fake — one-hot vectors \(e_i \in \mathbb{R}^E\) — so that \(y_t\) literally writes the gate vector into the columns chosen by \(\mathcal{T}_t\), and the diagnostic is a single allclose.

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

# Step 1: hand-coded router scores for 4 tokens over 4 experts.
scores = torch.tensor(
    [[ 2.0,  0.3,  1.5, -1.0],     # cat
     [ 0.5,  2.5,  0.2,  1.0],     # sat
     [-0.5,  1.2,  2.0,  0.8],     # code
     [ 0.1,  0.7,  0.4,  1.9]],    # runs
)                                  # shape: (N=4, E=4)

# Step 2: top-K selection.
topk_values, indices = torch.topk(scores, k=2, dim=-1)   # both (N, K)

# Step 3: softmax over the K selected scores only.
gates = F.softmax(topk_values, dim=-1)                   # (N, K), rows sum to 1

# Step 4: weighted combine over the selected experts.
expert_outputs = torch.eye(scores.shape[-1])             # (E, D=E) one-hot stand-in
selected = expert_outputs[indices]                       # (N, K, D)
y = (gates.unsqueeze(-1) * selected).sum(dim=1)          # (N, D)

# Diagnostic: gates sum to 1 per token; combine reads out the gate matrix.
assert torch.allclose(gates.sum(dim=-1), torch.ones(4))
assert torch.isclose(y[0, 0], gates[0, 0]) and torch.isclose(y[0, 2], gates[0, 1])

Running the script under examples/ch01/ prints the score matrix, the top-\(K\) indices, and the gate matrix:

token indices gates cat 0 2 0.622 0.378 sat 1 3 0.818 0.182 code 2 1 0.690 0.310 runs 3 1 0.769 0.231

Every row of the gate column sums to one. With one-hot expert outputs, the combined tensor is the same matrix rewritten into the columns named by indices; rows still sum to one. That last property is the section's diagnostic: any error in the softmax-over-selected step (taking it over all \(E\), normalising twice, forgetting to gather the selected values) breaks it.

Diagnostic. Check that gates for each token sum to one after top-\(K\) normalization. Run python examples/ch01/section_1_3_a_tiny_routing_story.py and verify the printed "Row sums of gates" line is all ones, then pytest tests/ch01/ -q should report at least 10 new tests covering shape, sum-to-one, top-\(K\) identity, and the combine read-out.

This toy flow becomes the shape contract for every later implementation.

docs.title: 1.4 What from scratch means for this book
docs.text:
Sections 1.2 and 1.3 introduced two new objects — a router and a per-token gate — and the temptation now is to reach for a library that wraps both behind a single call. We will not do that. The point of this book is the opposite: every tensor that crosses an MoE boundary is named, shaped, and assertable, and every line of model code mirrors a listing the reader has already read. A one-line library call hides the failure mode at the centre of MoE engineering (whose gates? which experts? how is the bias used?); a transparent router–dispatch–expert–combine pipeline exposes it. The price is that we write more code; the payoff is that we can debug what we wrote.

Figure 1.4 — The build ladder. Each rung is concrete and tested before we climb to the next: hand-built tensors first, vectorized PyTorch next, then training scripts and the assembled reference model. Rendered via TikZ in the PDF version.

  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Rung 1  Scalar / by-hand                       │  Section 1.3
  │   4 tokens, 4 experts, top-2 picked by pencil  │
  └───────────────────────┬────────────────────────┘
                          ▲
  ┌───────────────────────┴────────────────────────┐
  │ Rung 2  Vectorized PyTorch                     │  Chapters 3–9
  │   torch.topk, F.softmax, batched dispatch      │
  └───────────────────────┬────────────────────────┘
                          ▲
  ┌───────────────────────┴────────────────────────┐
  │ Rung 3  Training & smoke tests                 │  Chapters 10–12
  │   examples/, tests/, validator, dashboards     │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  Contract: every section ships
  .tex + .md + figure + table + equation + listing + code + example + test
  Out of scope: kernels, distributed schedulers, deploy.

Figure 1.4 draws the build as a three-rung ladder with a banner naming the contract and a strip naming the explicit out-of-scope. The build proceeds in three rungs. The first is the by-hand example we just finished in Section 1.3: a \((4, 4)\) score matrix, top-\(K\) chosen by inspection, gates printed as decimals. The second is vectorized PyTorch: the same logic written with torch.topk, F.softmax, batched dispatch into expert MLPs, and a weighted combine. The third is the assembled reference model and the things you do with it once it runs: training script, smoke tests, dashboards. We climb the ladder one rung at a time so each rung is testable on its own.

Before declaring any new class, take inventory of what is already named. Sections 1.1–1.3 introduced \(B, T, D, H, N\); the constants \(E\) (routed experts) and \(K\) (top-\(K\)); and three tensors — router scores \(s \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times E}\), the index set \(\mathcal{T}_t \subset \{1,\dots,E\}\) of size \(K\), and the gate matrix \(g \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times K}\). With those names settled, the rest of the book lives inside one promise: the MoE layer keeps the decoder interface intact.

Table 1.4 — The from-scratch contract for this book. Left column: what every chapter delivers. Middle: how each deliverable is verified. Right: what we leave to other resources.

Section validator + checklist_from_index(...).is_complete(). Slide decks; survey writing; multi-paper comparisons. Tensor shapes Every tensor name and rank is fixed before the listing it appears in. The decoder interface stays \((B, T, D) \to (B, T, D)\). MoEInterface wraps subclass _forward and raises RuntimeError on shape drift. Production attention kernels, fused dispatch ops. That interface is the only equation Chapter 1 actually pins down — everything else in the book is filling it in.

\[ \mathrm{MoELayer}\colon\; \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times D} \;\longrightarrow\; \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times D}, \qquad \bigl(\mathrm{MoELayer}(x)\bigr).\mathtt{shape} \;=\; x.\mathtt{shape} \quad\text{for every concrete implementation in Chapters 3--10.} \]

The equation says exactly two things. First, every MoELayer in this book is a drop-in replacement for the dense FFN of Section 1.1: same input shape, same output shape. Second, this is not just a comment in a docstring — the listing below builds it into a base class that wraps subclass implementations with a runtime assertion. A subclass that drops or duplicates tokens raises RuntimeError immediately; a caller that hands a wrong-rank tensor raises ValueError.

class MoEInterface(nn.Module, ABC):
    # Every MoE block honours (B, T, D) -> (B, T, D).
    def __init__(self, d_model):
        super().__init__(); self.d_model = d_model

    @abstractmethod
    def _forward(self, x): ...

    def forward(self, x):
        if x.ndim != 3 or x.shape[-1] != self.d_model:
            raise ValueError(f"expected (B, T, {self.d_model}); got {tuple(x.shape)}")
        y = self._forward(x)
        if y.shape != x.shape:
            raise RuntimeError(f"interface violation: {tuple(x.shape)} != {tuple(y.shape)}")
        return y

class Router(nn.Module):           # x (B,T,D) -> scores (N, E).   Built in Ch. 3.2.
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_experts): ...
    def forward(self, x): raise NotImplementedError

class ExpertMLP(nn.Module):        # x (*, D) -> y (*, D).         Built in Ch. 3.1.
    def __init__(self, d_model, hidden): ...
    def forward(self, x): raise NotImplementedError

class MoELayer(MoEInterface):      # Top-K routed FFN.             Built in Ch. 3-6.
    def __init__(self, d_model, hidden, n_experts, top_k): ...
    def _forward(self, x): raise NotImplementedError

class MiniDeepSeekMoE(MoEInterface):   # Reference model.          Assembled in Ch. 10.
    def __init__(self, d_model, hidden, n_experts, top_k, n_shared): ...
    def _forward(self, x): raise NotImplementedError

The listing declares the four objects every later chapter will fill in: Router (Chapter 3.2), ExpertMLP (Chapter 3.1), MoELayer (Chapters 3–6), and MiniDeepSeekMoE (Chapter 10). All four exist in src/moe_from_scratch/ch01/from_scratch_skeleton.py today and instantiate cleanly; their forward methods raise NotImplementedError until the chapter that builds them. The skeleton is what we hand to readers who jump to Chapter 7: they can read the interface without skimming Chapters 3–6.

The diagnostic for this section is meta. Section 1.4 promises that every section in the book ships a fixed set of artifacts; the diagnostic is a function that verifies the promise on a real section. The example script under examples/ch01/ runs checklist_from_index against the section index for Section 1.1 and asserts that all eleven items (section .tex, section .md, chapter.tex, chapter.md, figure, table, listing, equation, code, example, test) are present. It then runs the same check on Section 4.1 (the first section of Chapter 4, not yet drafted) and confirms that the checklist correctly reports md as missing, so a not-yet-drafted section cannot silently masquerade as done.

Diagnostic. Checklist that every chapter must include shapes, a code path, and a verification artifact. Run python examples/ch01/section_1_4_from_scratch_contract.py and verify Section 1.1 reports OK for all eleven items while Section 4.1 reports missing = ['md', 'code', 'example', 'test']. Then pytest tests/ch01/ -q should add at least 20 new tests covering skeleton instantiation, interface assertions, and the checklist's correctness against the live repository.

With the boundary defined, we can plan the exact model we will build.

docs.title: 1.5 The MiniDeepSeekMoE build ladder
docs.text:
Section 1.4 declared four skeleton classes and an interface invariant; what it did not do is name the order in which we fill them in or the model we are aiming at. This section does both. The target model is MiniDeepSeekMoE-16x2: six decoder layers, model width \(256\), sixteen routed experts per MoE layer with top-\(K=2\), one shared expert that always runs. We will not write that model first. We will start from a much smaller smoke configuration — two layers, four routed experts, one shared expert — and grow it one rung at a time, keeping a runnable diagnostic at every rung.

Figure 1.5 — The build ladder. Twelve rungs from the dense baseline (Ch. 2) up to inference and scaling (Ch. 12). Colour groups: dense (gray), routed top-\(K\) (purple), capacity / load (gold), shared experts and bias balancing (green), evaluation (red). Smoke config runs from Ch. 3; MiniDeepSeekMoE-16x2 is operational at Ch. 10. Rendered via TikZ in the PDF version.

  Ch.12  Inference, performance, scaling                              ◄─ MiniDeepSeekMoE-16x2
  Ch.11  Training, diagnostics, ablation matrix                          fully operational
  Ch.10  Assemble MiniDeepSeekMoE end-to-end                          ◄──┘
  Ch. 9  Auxiliary-loss-free balancing  (biased select, unbiased combine)
  Ch. 8  Shared + fine-grained routed experts
  Ch. 7  Router training: aux + z loss
  Ch. 6  Vectorized dispatch + capacity
  Ch. 5  Top-2 routing, weighted combine
  Ch. 4  Top-1 routing, Switch-style dispatch
  Ch. 3  First MoE layer: Router, ExpertMLP, naive dispatch           ◄─ Smoke config
  Ch. 2  Dense Transformer baseline (attention + dense FFN)              runs from here
  Ch. 1  (here)  shapes, contract, build ladder

Figure 1.5 colours the rungs by build phase: gray for the dense baseline, purple for routed top-\(K\), gold for capacity and load, green for shared experts and bias balancing, red for evaluation and inference. Begin at the bottom of the ladder. Chapter 2 builds the dense Transformer baseline: tokenizer, embeddings, causal self-attention, the dense FFN whose cost we already counted in Section 1.1, and a training loop that runs on a laptop. The MoE layer has nowhere to live without that scaffold, and Chapter 2's diagnostic — a loss curve that decreases on a tiny dataset — becomes the comparison point for every later experiment. From there the ladder climbs through routed experts (Ch. 3–6), training stabilisers (Ch. 7), shared and fine-grained experts (Ch. 8), and auxiliary-loss-free balancing (Ch. 9) before the full model is assembled in Chapter 10. Chapters 11 and 12 are evaluation and inference rather than construction; they consume the model rather than add to it.

The notation does not change at the top of the ladder; it only adds two symbols. We keep \(B, T, D, N, E, K\) from earlier sections. Chapter 8 introduces \(S\), the number of shared experts (always \(\ge 0\); the book uses \(S=1\)). Chapter 9 introduces a router-bias buffer \(b \in \mathbb{R}^E\) that nudges expert selection without entering the gate-weighted combine. The full forward equation for one MoE layer follows.

\[ y_t \;=\; \underbrace{x_t}_{\text{residual (Ch.\,2)}} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{j=1}^{S} \mathrm{shared}_j(x_t)}_{\text{shared experts (Ch.\,8)}} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}_t} g_{t,i}\, \mathrm{routed}_i(x_t)}_{\text{top-}K\text{ routed experts (Ch.\,3-6)}}, \] \[ \mathcal{T}_t \;=\; \operatorname*{top\,K}_i\,(s_{t,i} + b_i), \qquad g_{t,i} \;=\; \operatorname{softmax}_{i \in \mathcal{T}_t}(s_{t,i}) \quad \text{(unbiased, Ch.\,9).} \]

The equation packs the entire build into one line. The residual \(x_t\) comes from Chapter 2. The shared-expert sum \(\sum_{j=1}^{S} \mathrm{shared}_j(x_t)\) comes online in Chapter 8 and runs for every token regardless of routing. The routed-expert combine \(\sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}_t} g_{t,i}\,\mathrm{routed}_i(x_t)\) is built up across Chapters 3–6, weighted by gates that we already computed by hand in Section 1.3. The two annotations under \(\mathcal{T}_t\) and \(g_{t,i}\) are the only subtle part: the top-\(K\) selection uses the biased score \(s_{t,i} + b_i\) (Chapter 9), but the gates are softmax over the unbiased selected scores \(s_{t,i}\). That asymmetry is the MiniDeepSeekMoE invariant we will protect for the rest of the book.

Table 1.5 — Chapter-by-chapter milestones for MiniDeepSeekMoE. Each row names the build step, what it adds to the layer, and the falsifiable diagnostic that lands in that chapter (mirrored in chapter_milestones()).

Ch. Build step What enters the model Diagnostic that lands 1 From dense to conditional compute Notation, ladder, contract. \(\alpha = K/E\) matches book equation; shapes pass. 2 Dense Transformer baseline Tokenizer, embeddings, attention, dense FFN. Generation runs; loss decreases on tiny dataset. 3 Experts, routers, first MoE layer ExpertMLP, Router, naive dispatch. Naive MoE matches a hand-built routing-story tensor. 4 Top-1 routing, Switch-style dispatch Assignment masks, expert buckets, capacity drops. Load histogram + dropped-token count reported. 5 Top-2 routing, weighted combine Two-expert paths, normalized gates. Per-token gates sum to \(1\); top-2 beats top-1 on toy loss. 6 Vectorized dispatch + capacity Flattened token batch, capacity factor, overflow. Vectorized layer matches naive layer within tolerance. 7 Router training, load-balancing losses Auxiliary load loss, z-loss, dashboards. Aux+z-loss reduce expert-load variance during training. 8 Shared + fine-grained routed experts Shared expert path, segmented routed experts. Shared-only ablates against routed-only; both contribute. 9 Auxiliary-loss-free balancing Router bias buffer; biased select, unbiased combine. Bias affects selection only; combine stays unbiased. 10 Assembling end-to-end Config object, decoder block, training/sampling. Full forward \((B,T,D) \to (B,T,D)\); loss-dict keys stable. 11 Training, diagnostics, experiments Ablation matrix, loss curves, expert-behaviour plots. Ablation produces consistent loss-curve dashboard. 12 Inference, performance, scaling Active-parameter accounting, expert parallelism map. Active-parameter accounting matches measured FLOPs/token.

The table maps each chapter to its build step and its falsifiable diagnostic. The diagnostic column matters: Section 1.4 promised that every section ships a runnable check, and the build ladder promises that every chapter ships one of these milestone diagnostics on top of the section-level ones.

Both configurations are declared today. The smoke configuration is what the example script for this section instantiates so we can read off the active fraction and the activated-parameter count; MiniDeepSeekMoE-16x2 is declared alongside it as a forward reference.

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class MiniDeepSeekMoEConfig:
    name: str
    d_model: int           # D
    hidden: int            # H
    n_layers: int
    n_heads: int
    n_routed_experts: int  # E
    top_k: int             # K
    n_shared_experts: int  # S  (>= 0)
    vocab_size: int
    context_length: int

    @property
    def active_fraction(self) -> float:     # K / E (Section 1.2)
        return self.top_k / self.n_routed_experts

SMOKE_CONFIG = MiniDeepSeekMoEConfig(
    name="MiniDeepSeekMoE-Smoke",
    d_model=64,  hidden=128,  n_layers=2, n_heads=4,
    n_routed_experts=4, top_k=2, n_shared_experts=1,
    vocab_size=2048, context_length=64,
)

MAIN_CONFIG_16X2 = MiniDeepSeekMoEConfig(
    name="MiniDeepSeekMoE-16x2",
    d_model=256, hidden=512, n_layers=6, n_heads=8,
    n_routed_experts=16, top_k=2, n_shared_experts=1,
    vocab_size=8192, context_length=256,
)

assert SMOKE_CONFIG.active_fraction      == 0.5     # K=2, E=4
assert MAIN_CONFIG_16X2.active_fraction  == 0.125   # K=2, E=16

The constructor enforces every constraint Section 1.4 said the interface needs: positive sizes, \(K \le E\), \(S \ge 0\), \(D\) divisible by the number of attention heads. The example script under examples/ch01/ prints both configurations, the active fraction \(K/E\), and the chapter milestones in order; the matching tests under tests/ch01/ pin those numbers down so a future config edit cannot silently drift.

Diagnostic. Milestone checklist that marks which diagnostics appear by each chapter. Run python examples/ch01/section_1_5_build_ladder.py and verify the printed active fractions (\(0.5\) for the smoke config; \(0.125\) for MiniDeepSeekMoE-16x2), the activated expert-parameter counts \((K+S)\cdot 2 D H\) for both, and the twelve milestone rows in chapter order \(1 \to 12\). Then pytest tests/ch01/ -q should add at least 20 new tests covering config invariants, parameter-scaling properties, and milestone integrity.

The first build step is a dense Transformer baseline that gives the MoE layer somewhere to live.

docs.title: 1.6 Chapter summary and handoff
docs.text:
Section 1.5 named the destination — MiniDeepSeekMoE-16x2 — and the twelve-rung path to it. Before climbing, take stock: Chapter 1 introduced fifteen symbols, four skeleton classes, two configurations, a twelve-rung build ladder, and one decoder-interface invariant. The risk now is that any of that drifts as the implementation gets bigger. This section closes the chapter by writing the vocabulary down in one place, locking the skeleton constructors with a runtime signature check, and answering the question that determines whether the build ladder is well-posed at all: which part of the dense decoder block are we actually replacing?

Figure 1.6 — Concept map for Chapter 1. Every node carries the symbol and shape that the rest of the book will use. The grey panel lists what stays the same when MoE moves in; the green panel names the single sub-layer that is replaced. Rendered via TikZ in the PDF version.

  ┌────────┐    ┌────────┐    ┌─────────┐
  │ tokens │───►│ Router │───►│ top-K   │
  │ (B,T,D)│    │ s (N,E)│    │ T_t (N,K)
  └────────┘    └────────┘    └────┬────┘
        ▲                          │
        │                  ┌───────┴────────┐
        │                  ▼                ▼
        │            ┌─────────┐     ┌─────────────┐
        │            │ experts │◄────│  softmax    │
        │            │ (sel.)  │     │  g (N,K)    │
        │            └────┬────┘     │  Σ g = 1    │
        │                 │          └─────────────┘
        │                 ▼
        │            ┌─────────┐                ┌──────── KEPT in Ch. 2–10 ────────┐
        └────────────│  y      │                │ • residual                       │
                     │ (B,T,D) │                │ • self-attention                 │
                     └─────────┘                │ • (B,T,D) decoder interface      │
                                                └──────────────────────────────────┘
                                                ┌──────── REPLACED (Ch.3–10) ──────┐
                                                │ • ONLY the dense FFN sub-layer   │
                                                └──────────────────────────────────┘

Figure 1.6 is the chapter on one page: tokens enter on the left, the router–top-\(K\)–softmax pipeline lives in the middle, the output exits on the right, and a side panel names what stays the same (residual, attention, \((B,T,D)\) interface) and what gets replaced (the dense FFN, and only that). The four-token example from Section 1.3 carries every symbol the rest of the book needs. With \(N = 4\) tokens, \(E = 4\) experts, and \(K = 2\), that example produced a score tensor \(s\) of shape \((N, E) = (4, 4)\), an index set \(\mathcal{T}_t\) of shape \((N, K) = (4, 2)\), a gate tensor \(g\) of shape \((N, K) = (4, 2)\) with rows summing to one, and an output tensor of shape \((N, D) = (4, 4)\) that — because the experts were one-hot — literally read out the gate matrix. Chapters 2–10 will replace each of those tensors with a real computation, but the symbols and shapes will not move.

Table 1.6 — Chapter-1 first-use glossary. Every symbol below appears unchanged in the rest of the book; the Intro column points back to the section where it was defined.

Symbol Meaning Shape Code object Intro \(B\) batch size scalar x.shape[0] 1.1 \(T\) sequence length scalar x.shape[1] 1.1 \(D\) model width scalar config.d_model 1.1 \(H\) FFN hidden width scalar config.hidden 1.1 \(N\) flattened token count scalar \(B\,T\) 1.1 \(E\) routed expert count scalar config.n_routed_experts 1.2 \(K\) experts per token scalar config.top_k 1.2 \(S\) shared expert count scalar config.n_shared_experts 1.5 \(\alpha\) active fraction \(K/E\) scalar config.active_fraction 1.2 \(x\) block input \((B,T,D)\) x: Tensor 1.1 \(s\) router scores \((N,E)\) story.scores 1.3 \(\mathcal{T}_t\) top-\(K\) index set \((N,K)\) story.indices 1.3 \(g\) selected gates \((N,K)\) story.gates 1.3 \(b\) router bias buffer \((E,)\) Ch. 9 router state 1.5 \(y\) block output \((B,T,D)\) MoELayer(x) 1.4

The shape pipeline of the layer fits in one equation.

\[ \underbrace{x}_{(B,T,D)} \;\xrightarrow{\text{Router}}\; \underbrace{s}_{(N,E)} \;\xrightarrow{\operatorname{top}K}\; \underbrace{\mathcal{T}}_{(N,K)} \;\xrightarrow{\operatorname{softmax}}\; \underbrace{g}_{(N,K)} \;\xrightarrow{\sum g_{t,i}\,\mathrm{expert}_i(x_t)}\; \underbrace{y}_{(B,T,D)}, \quad N = B\,T,\;\; \mathcal{T}_t \subset \{1,\dots,E\},\;\; \textstyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}_t} g_{t,i} = 1 . \]

The equation reads left-to-right: tokens \(x\) go into the router and become scores \(s\); top-\(K\) selects an index set \(\mathcal{T}\); softmax over the selected entries produces gates \(g\); the weighted combine of expert outputs lands at \(y\), of the same shape as \(x\). Every arrow is the title of a section we have already seen.

The chapter is held together by two pieces of code. The first locks the constructors of the four skeleton classes so that later chapters cannot quietly change the contract; the second answers the reader checkpoint by walking the decoder paths and asserting that only one is replaced.

def required_signatures():
    # Lock the constructor signatures every later chapter must keep.
    return {
        Router:          ("self", "d_model", "n_experts"),
        ExpertMLP:       ("self", "d_model", "hidden"),
        MoELayer:        ("self", "d_model", "hidden", "n_experts", "top_k"),
        MiniDeepSeekMoE: ("self", "d_model", "hidden", "n_experts", "top_k", "n_shared"),
    }

def check_signatures():
    for cls, expected in required_signatures().items():
        actual = tuple(inspect.signature(cls.__init__).parameters.keys())
        if actual != expected:
            raise AssertionError(f"{cls.__name__} drifted: {actual} != {expected}")

def moe_replaces_only_ffn():
    # Reader checkpoint: residual and attention stay; the FFN is what swaps.
    replaced = [p for p in decoder_replacement_plan() if p.replaced_by_moe]
    return len(replaced) == 1 and replaced[0].path == "FFN"

check_signatures()                # locked-in API survives
assert moe_replaces_only_ffn()    # the (B,T,D) interface is preserved by Ch.2-10

The signature check uses inspect.signature on Router.__init__, ExpertMLP.__init__, MoELayer.__init__, and MiniDeepSeekMoE.__init__ and raises AssertionError on any drift. The replacement check returns True when exactly one decoder path is marked replaced and that path is the FFN; if a future chapter ever marks attention or the residual as replaceable, the predicate will fail and the diagnostic will catch the contradiction with the chapter-level invariant.

Diagnostic. Reader checkpoint: identify which part of the dense model will be replaced by MoE. Run python examples/ch01/section_1_6_chapter_summary.py and verify that the glossary lists 15 symbols, the four-token story prints with \(s\in(4,4)\), \(\mathcal{T}\in(4,2)\), \(g\in(4,2)\), \(y\in(4,4)\), the signature check passes silently, and the replacement plan reports REPLACED only on the FFN row. Then pytest tests/ch01/ -q should report at least 11 new tests (89 total in Chapter 1) covering glossary integrity, signature parity, and the FFN-only predicate.

Next we build the dense decoder baseline so the replacement is meaningful.

docs.title: 2.1 Dataset and token batches
docs.text:
Chapter 1 ended with a contract: MoE will replace the FFN sub-layer of a dense decoder block, keep the \((B, T, D)\) decoder interface, and stay falsifiable at every rung of the ladder. Before the first expert can be wired in, that dense block needs an input to consume. This chapter builds the dense baseline; this section builds its data pipeline. The whole pipeline lives behind one function, get_batch, which returns a \((B, T)\) tensor of input token IDs and a parallel \((B, T)\) tensor of target IDs shifted by one position. Every later model variant in the book — top-1, top-2, shared experts, MiniDeepSeekMoE — consumes batches with exactly these shapes.

Figure 2.1 — Four stages of the chapter-2 data pipeline: text → tokenized stream → train/val split → random-offset slicing into \((B, T)\) input and target windows. The arrows under the two rows show the one-position shift that makes target[t] equal to input[t+1] on every row. Rendered via TikZ in the PDF version.

1. text       "the cat sat on the mat the dog ran ..."
                                  │
                                  ▼
2. tokenize   tokenizer.encode(text)   →  tokens  shape (N_tokens,)
                                  │
                       ┌──────────┴──────────┐
                       ▼                     ▼
3a. train (90%)                       3b. val (10%)
   shape (N_train,)                     shape (N_val,)
                       │
                       ▼   get_batch(train, B=2, T=8) samples B start offsets s_b:
        ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
input    │ t  h  e  ␣  c  a  t  ␣ │   s_0 to s_0+T-1
        └──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬───┘
           │  │  │  │  │  │  │
           ▼  ▼  ▼  ▼  ▼  ▼  ▼
        ┌──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┐
target   │ h  e  ␣  c  a  t  ␣  s │   s_0+1 to s_0+T
        └─────────────────────────┘

         target[:, t] == input[:, t+1]   for t ∈ {0,...,T-2}

Take the chapter's anchor mini-example: \(B = 2\) samples, \(T = 8\) tokens per sample. We tokenize a short corpus, split tail \(10\%\) for validation, sample two random start offsets from the train half, and slice two parallel windows of length \(T\) at each offset. The reference corpus is deliberately written from cat, sat, code, runs (the four words from Section 1.3) so the reader can carry the same vocabulary across chapters.

Name the new symbols before writing the equation. We keep \(B\) (batch size) and \(T\) (sequence length, also called the block size) from Chapter 1. Two new constants enter the book here: \(V\), the vocabulary size — the number of distinct token IDs the tokenizer emits, used as the row count of the embedding matrix in Section 2.2 and the column count of the language-model head; and \(N_{\text{tokens}} = N_{\text{train}} + N_{\text{val}}\), the length of the token stream after splitting. The model width \(D\) from Chapter 1 has not appeared yet — it enters at the embedding step.

Table 2.1 — Tensor contract for the chapter-2 data pipeline. Every later model variant consumes batches with exactly these shapes.

Tensor name Shape Created by Used by Failure check tokens \((N_{\text{tokens}},)\) long tokenizer.encode(text) make_split (train / val), get_batch tokens.dtype == torch.long; all IDs \(< V\). train, val \((N_{\text{train}},)\), \((N_{\text{val}},)\) long make_split(text, val_fraction) get_batch \(N_{\text{train}} + N_{\text{val}} = N_{\text{tokens}}\); both non-zero. input_ids \((B, T)\) long get_batch(train, B, T) Section 2.2 embeddings Each row decodes to a contiguous slice of the source text. target_ids \((B, T)\) long get_batch(train, B, T) Next-token cross-entropy loss (Section 2.5) Falsifiable: target[:, :-1] == input[:, 1:]. Failure mode — reuse same start offset for input/target — Loss becomes trivial (predict the token you already saw); shift check fires.

The next-token objective is purely an indexing relation between two slices of the same stream.

\[ \mathrm{input}_{b,t} \;=\; \mathtt{tokens}[s_b + t], \qquad \mathrm{target}_{b,t} \;=\; \mathtt{tokens}[s_b + t + 1], \qquad\text{so}\qquad \boxed{\;\mathrm{target}_{b,t} \;=\; \mathrm{input}_{b,t+1}\;} \quad\text{for } t \in \{0,1,\dots,T{-}2\}. \]

The equation says exactly one thing: input and target are slices of the same token stream that differ by a single position. The boxed identity target[t] == input[t+1] for \(t \in \{0, \dots, T{-}2\}\) is the section's falsifiable diagnostic. Break the +1 on the target slice — accidentally pass the same start offset for both — and the identity fails on every row.

The listing realises the equation in seven lines of PyTorch. It mirrors src/moe_from_scratch/ch02/dataset.py exactly, including the function name get_batch and the keyword-only generator parameter we use to make the example script reproducible.

def get_batch(tokens, *, batch_size, block_size, generator=None):
    # tokens: (N_tokens,) long stream from make_split(text).train.
    n = tokens.shape[0]
    high = n - block_size
    starts = torch.randint(0, high, (batch_size,), generator=generator)
    input_ids  = torch.stack([tokens[s     : s + block_size    ] for s in starts])
    target_ids = torch.stack([tokens[s + 1 : s + 1 + block_size] for s in starts])
    return input_ids, target_ids       # both (B, T)

# Mini-example: B=2, T=8 over the chapter-2 reference corpus (cat, sat, code, runs).
split = make_split(REFERENCE_CORPUS, val_fraction=0.1)
gen   = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)
x, y  = get_batch(split.train, batch_size=2, block_size=8, generator=gen)
assert torch.equal(y[:, :-1], x[:, 1:])   # target[:, t] == input[:, t+1]

Running the example script under examples/ch02/ on the reference corpus prints a 19-character vocabulary, 162 train tokens, 18 val tokens, and then a \((2, 8)\) batch. With seed \(0\) the first input row decodes to "an on th" and the corresponding target row decodes to "n on the" — the target is the input shifted left by one character, which is exactly what the equation promises. The final assert in the script checks the shift identity on both rows of the batch at once via torch.equal(target[:, :-1], input[:, 1:]); the pytest suite under tests/ch02/ adds an independent random-seed check and rejects bad inputs (zero block_size, 2-D tokens, etc.).

Diagnostic. Print the first input-target pair and decode it to verify shifting. Run python examples/ch02/section_2_1_dataset_and_token_batches.py and verify the printed lines: vocab has 19 characters; train tokens: 162; val tokens: 18; the seed-0 first input row decodes to "an on th" and the first target row decodes to "n on the"; the closing assertion target[:, t] == input[:, t+1] passes. Then pytest tests/ch02/ -q should report at least 11 new tests (ch02 11/11) covering the tokenizer round trip, train/val split shapes, batch shapes, the shift identity, seed determinism, and input validation.

Token IDs become vectors through embeddings and positions.

docs.title: 2.2 Token and position embeddings
docs.text:
Section 2.1 produced \((B, T)\) tensors of integer token IDs. Every downstream module — attention, the dense FFN of Section 2.4, and the MoE replacements in Chapters 3–10 — expects floats, not integers, and expects the decoder interface \((B, T, D)\) that Chapter 1 promised. The embedding step bridges the two. It is also the first place the model width \(D\) from Chapter 1 actually appears.

Figure 2.2 — Two table lookups, summed. Each integer in input_ids indexes one row of the token table \(E_{\text{tok}}\); the positions \(0, 1, \dots, T{-}1\) index one row of the position table \(E_{\text{pos}}\); the two \((D,)\) vectors are summed elementwise. The position lookup is the only piece of information that distinguishes the same token appearing at two different times. Rendered via TikZ in the PDF version.

                                          ┌──────────────────┐
input_ids (B,T) ─── token IDs ──────────► │  E_tok (V, D)    │
   row 0: [1, 12, 0, 13, 12, 0, 16, 8]    │  lookup per ID   │ ──┐
   row 1: [0,  6, 10, 9,  5, 15, 0, 6]    └──────────────────┘   │
                                                                  ├─►  (+)  ─►  x  (B, T, D)
                positions 0..T-1          ┌──────────────────┐   │
                  (broadcast over batch)  │  E_pos (T_max, D)│ ──┘
                                          │  lookup per t    │
                                          └──────────────────┘
              x[b, t]  =  E_tok[ ids[b, t] ]  +  E_pos[ t ]

Keep the chapter-2 anchor mini-example: \(B = 2\), \(T = 8\). Section 2.1 produced a \((2, 8)\) input_ids batch with vocabulary size \(V = 19\) from the reference corpus. Pick the model width \(D = 16\) and the maximum context length \(T_{\max} = 8\) (the same as the block size we used for batching), and the two embedding tables hold \(V D + T_{\max} D = 19 \cdot 16 + 8 \cdot 16 = 304 + 128 = 432\) parameters.

Name the new symbols. We keep \(B\) (batch size), \(T\) (sequence length), and \(V\) (vocab size) from Section 2.1. The model width \(D\) enters the book here for the first time as a live tensor dimension (it was declared in Chapter 1 but no module had it yet). One more constant appears: \(T_{\max}\), the maximum context length the position table supports; a \((B, T)\) batch with \(T \le T_{\max}\) slices into the top \(T\) rows of \(E_{\text{pos}}\).

Table 2.2 — Tensor and parameter contract for the chapter-2 embeddings. With the reference-corpus vocabulary (\(V=19\)), \(D=16\), \(T_{\max}=8\), the two tables hold \(304 + 128 = 432\) parameters.

Tensor name Shape Created by Used by Failure check token_embed.weight \(E_{\text{tok}}\) \((V, D)\) float nn.Embedding(V, D) Row lookup for every \(\mathrm{input\_ids}_{b,t}\). Backward through a non-zero output assigns gradient to at least the rows of observed token IDs. position_embed.weight \(E_{\text{pos}}\) \((T_{\max}, D)\) float nn.Embedding(T_max, D) Row lookup for every position \(t \in \{0,\dots,T-1\}\). A \(T\)-long batch produces non-zero grad on rows \(0..T-1\) and zero grad on rows \(T..T_{\max}-1\). input_ids \((B, T)\) long get_batch (Section 2.1) Indexing into \(E_{\text{tok}}\). input_ids.dtype == torch.long; rank \(== 2\); entries \(< V\). x (embedded sequence) \((B, T, D)\) float TokenPositionEmbedding(...)(input_ids) Causal self-attention (Section 2.3); decoder block. Falsifiable: x.shape == (B, T, D) and gradients reach BOTH tables on backward. Failure mode — dropping either summand — One of the two *.weight.grad tensors is all-zero; the diagnostic fires.

The forward pass is one tensor equation that names every shape.

\[ x_{b,t} \;=\; \underbrace{E_{\text{tok}}\bigl[\mathrm{input\_ids}_{b,t}\bigr]}_{\text{token table lookup}} \;+\; \underbrace{E_{\text{pos}}[t]}_{\text{position table lookup}} \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{D}, \qquad E_{\text{tok}} \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times D}, \;\; E_{\text{pos}} \in \mathbb{R}^{T_{\max} \times D}, \;\; x \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times D}. \]

The equation packs the entire step into one line, but two details matter. First, the position lookup is shared across the batch: \(E_{\text{pos}}[t]\) depends only on the position index \(t\), not on the row \(b\), so the same \(T\) vectors are added to every row of the batch (broadcast). Second, the sum is the only operator that connects the two tables. Drop one summand and the corresponding table receives no gradient at all — which is exactly what the diagnostic checks.

The implementation mirrors the equation one line at a time. It lives in src/moe_from_scratch/ch02/embedding.py as TokenPositionEmbedding, an nn.Module whose constructor takes the three sizes (\(V\), \(D\), \(T_{\max}\)) and whose forward returns a \((B, T, D)\) tensor.

class TokenPositionEmbedding(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size, d_model, context_length):
        super().__init__()
        self.token_embed    = nn.Embedding(vocab_size,     d_model)   # E_tok: (V,     D)
        self.position_embed = nn.Embedding(context_length, d_model)   # E_pos: (T_max, D)
        self.context_length = context_length

    def forward(self, input_ids):                                     # (B, T) long
        T = input_ids.shape[1]
        assert T <= self.context_length
        positions = torch.arange(T, device=input_ids.device)          # (T,)
        return self.token_embed(input_ids) + self.position_embed(positions)  # (B, T, D)

# Mini-example (chapter-2 anchor): V=19, D=16, T=8, B=2.
embed = TokenPositionEmbedding(vocab_size=19, d_model=16, context_length=8)
x     = embed(input_ids)                          # input_ids from get_batch(...)
assert x.shape == (2, 8, 16)
x.sum().backward()
assert embed.token_embed.weight.grad.abs().sum()    > 0
assert embed.position_embed.weight.grad.abs().sum() > 0

The example script under examples/ch02/ threads the seed-0 batch from Section 2.1 into the module, prints the parameter counts (\(304 + 128 = 432\)), checks the output shape, runs x.sum().backward(), and verifies that both embed.token_embed.weight.grad and embed.position_embed.weight.grad have non-zero \(\ell_1\) norm. With this batch and seed both grads have \(\ell_1\) norm exactly \(256\) (each summand contributes \(B \cdot T = 16\) ones to \(B \cdot T \cdot D = 256\) entries). The pytest suite under tests/ch02/ adds the closed-form check \(x_{b,t} = E_{\text{tok}}[\mathrm{ids}_{b,t}] + E_{\text{pos}}[t]\), asserts that the same token at two different positions produces different embeddings, and verifies that only the rows of \(E_{\text{tok}}\) corresponding to observed token IDs receive non-zero gradient.

Diagnostic. Assert output shape and confirm gradients flow to both embedding tables. Run python examples/ch02/section_2_2_token_and_position_embeddings.py and verify the printed lines: V=19, D=16, T_max=8; total = 432 parameters; x.shape = (2, 8, 16); \(|\text{token grad}|_1 = 256\) and \(|\text{pos grad}|_1 = 256\). Then pytest tests/ch02/ -q should add at least 12 new tests (ch02 23/23) covering size validation, forward shape, the same-token-different-position contrast, and the row-selective gradient pattern.

The embedded sequence now enters causal self-attention.

docs.title: 2.3 Causal self-attention as the context path
docs.text:
Section 2.2 produced a \((B, T, D)\) sequence in which every position carries its own embedded representation but no two positions can yet see each other. A decoder language model needs exactly one path that mixes information across positions — and exactly one rule that prevents that mixing from reaching forward in time. Self-attention is that path; the causal mask is that rule. Chapter 1 promised the FFN sub-layer would be the only thing we eventually swap for MoE; that promise relies on attention staying a fixed, minimal piece of the baseline, which is what we build here.

Figure 2.3 — One \(T \times T\) slice of multi-head causal attention. The raw scores \(QK^{\top}/\sqrt{d_{\text{head}}}\) are added to a mask whose strict upper triangle is \(-\infty\); the row-wise softmax drives those entries to exactly \(0\) while the lower-triangular weights sum to \(1\) per row. Row \(t\) becomes a probability distribution over positions \(\{0, \dots, t\}\) only. Rendered via TikZ in the PDF version.

  raw scores  Q K^T / sqrt(d_head)        causal mask M          masked scores         attn weights (after softmax)
       (T x T)                            (T x T)                (T x T)               (T x T)
   ┌─────────────────────┐                 0    -∞   -∞ ...      s   -∞  -∞  ...        w    0   0  ...    row sums = 1
   │ s  s  s  s  s  s  s s│                0    0   -∞ ...      s   s  -∞  ...        w    w   0  ...
   │ s  s  s  s  s  s  s s│                0    0    0  ...     s   s   s   ...       w    w   w  ...
   │ s  s  s  s  s  s  s s│         +      ...               =  ...                    ...
   │ s  s  s  s  s  s  s s│                                                            (token 0  sees only itself)
   │ s  s  s  s  s  s  s s│                                                            (token T-1 sees all)
   │ s  s  s  s  s  s  s s│
   │ s  s  s  s  s  s  s s│
   └─────────────────────┘
                                                          ▼
                                                row-wise softmax

Take the chapter-2 anchor mini-example: \(B = 2\), \(T = 8\), \(D = 16\). Pick \(n_h = 2\) attention heads, so \(d_{\text{head}} = D / n_h = 8\). One QKV projection (a single linear of width \(3D\)) plus one output projection (linear of width \(D\)) is all the parameter mass we need for this section — \(4 D^2 = 1024\) weights.

Name the new symbols. We keep \(B, T, D\) from Section 2.2 and \(T_{\max}\) from the embedding's position table. Three new symbols enter: \(n_h\), the number of heads; \(d_{\text{head}} = D / n_h\), the per-head channel width (the constructor refuses any \(D\) not divisible by \(n_h\)); and \(M \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times T}\), the additive causal mask whose upper triangle is \(-\infty\) and lower triangle (including the diagonal) is \(0\). The mask is registered as a buffer, not a parameter — it moves to the right device but never receives a gradient.

Table 2.3 — Tensor contract for one multi-head causal self-attention block. With the chapter-2 anchor (\(D=16\), \(n_h=2\), \(d_{\text{head}}=8\), \(T_{\max}=8\)), the block carries \(3 D^2\) QKV-projection weights and \(D^2\) output-projection weights.

Concept Shape Created by Why it matters Check \(x\) (input) \((B, T, D)\) Section 2.2 embeddings Decoder interface holds at every stage. Last axis \(= D\); rank \(= 3\). \(Q, K, V\) \((B, n_h, T, d_{\text{head}})\) qkv(x) chunk + reshape + transpose One linear of width \(3D\) split three ways; heads run in parallel. \(d_{\text{head}} = D / n_h\) is integer (constructor refuses otherwise). scores \((B, n_h, T, T)\) \(Q K^{\top} / \sqrt{d_{\text{head}}}\) Scale keeps softmax sharpness independent of head size. Numeric; pre-mask. attention weights \((B, n_h, T, T)\) \(\operatorname{softmax}(\text{scores} + M)\) Per-row probability distribution over visible positions only. Row sums \(= 1\); strict upper triangle \(= 0\). head output \((B, n_h, T, d_{\text{head}})\) weights \(@\,V\) Row \(t\) is a convex combination of \(V\)-rows \(0\ldots t\). Position \(t\) cannot mix anything past \(t\). \(y\) (output) \((B, T, D)\) out_proj(merge_heads(...)) Same shape as \(x\); ready for the residual sum and FFN sub-layer. Falsifiable: perturbing \(x[:, t, :]\) leaves \(y[:, :t, :]\) byte-identical. Failure mode — mask on wrong axis or applied after softmax — Past-output drift becomes non-zero; the diagnostic fires.

The block's tensor equation reads in one line.

\[ \mathrm{Attn}_h(x) \;=\; \operatorname{softmax}\!\left( \frac{Q_h K_h^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{\text{head}}}} \;+\; M \right)\, V_h, \qquad M_{t,s} = \begin{cases} 0 & s \le t,\\ -\infty & s > t,\end{cases} \qquad Q_h, K_h, V_h \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d_{\text{head}}},\;\; d_{\text{head}} = D / n_h. \]

The equation reads strictly left-to-right and the order matters: the mask \(M\) is added to the scaled scores before softmax, so the \(-\infty\) entries become exact zeros in the probability matrix — not small numbers that round to zero. Applying the mask after softmax (a common bug) would leave the probabilities renormalised over all \(T\) positions, then zero out the upper triangle without renormalising; the row sums would no longer equal one and gradients would still propagate from future tokens.

The implementation in src/moe_from_scratch/ch02/attention.py packs the equation into a small nn.Module. Two utility moves are worth flagging: a single Linear(D, 3D) produces \(Q\), \(K\), \(V\) in one matmul (then chunk), and the \((B, T, D) \to (B, n_h, T, d_{\text{head}})\) reshape happens by view + transpose, so heads run in parallel without an explicit loop.

class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads, context_length):
        super().__init__()
        assert d_model % n_heads == 0
        self.d_model = d_model
        self.n_heads = n_heads
        self.d_head  = d_model // n_heads
        self.qkv      = nn.Linear(d_model, 3 * d_model, bias=False)
        self.out_proj = nn.Linear(d_model,     d_model, bias=False)
        mask = torch.tril(torch.ones(context_length, context_length, dtype=torch.bool))
        self.register_buffer("causal_mask", mask, persistent=False)   # (T_max, T_max)

    def forward(self, x):                                              # (B, T, D)
        B, T, D = x.shape
        q, k, v = self.qkv(x).chunk(3, dim=-1)                         # each (B, T, D)
        # (B, T, D) -> (B, nh, T, d_head)
        split = lambda t: t.view(B, T, self.n_heads, self.d_head).transpose(1, 2)
        q, k, v = split(q), split(k), split(v)
        scores = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(self.d_head)    # (B, nh, T, T)
        scores = scores.masked_fill(~self.causal_mask[:T, :T], float("-inf"))
        attn   = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)                             # rows sum to 1
        out    = (attn @ v).transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(B, T, D)
        return self.out_proj(out)                                      # (B, T, D)

# Diagnostic: perturbing input position T-1 leaves outputs 0..T-2 byte-identical.
y       = attn(x)
xp      = x.clone(); xp[:, -1, :] = torch.randn(*xp[:, -1, :].shape)
yp      = attn(xp)
assert torch.equal(y[:, :-1, :], yp[:, :-1, :])         # past cannot see future

The section's diagnostic is the strongest possible end-to-end test of the mask: perturbing the input at position \(t\) must leave every output at positions \(s < t\) byte-identical. If the mask is missing, on the wrong axis, applied after softmax, or registered with the wrong shape, future-token information leaks back into the past and this diagnostic fires immediately. The example script under examples/ch02/ runs the chapter anchor batch through embeddings and then through CausalSelfAttention, perturbs only \(x[:, T{-}1, :]\) by a fresh random vector, and verifies that \(\max_{t < T-1} \lVert y_t - y_t' \rVert_\infty = 0\) exactly while the last-position drift is positive.

Diagnostic. Check that a token cannot attend to future positions. Run python examples/ch02/section_2_3_causal_self_attention.py and verify the printed lines: D=16 n_heads=2 d_head=8 T_max=8; attention input and output shapes both equal \((2, 8, 16)\); row sums of the attention weights equal \(1.0\) everywhere; strict-upper-triangle attention weight is exactly \(0\); max |y - y'| at positions \(0..T{-}2\) is 0.000e+00 and at position \(T{-}1\) is positive. Then pytest tests/ch02/ -q should add 18 new tests (ch02 41/41) covering construction, shape preservation, attention-row sums, the strict-upper-triangle property, the first-token-attends-only-to-itself check, the no-future-leak property at every \(t\), gradient flow through QKV and the output projection, and the mask-is-a-buffer-not-a-parameter check.

After attention mixes context, the dense FFN transforms each token independently.

docs.title: 2.4 Dense feed-forward block as the replacement target
docs.text:
Section 2.3 mixed positions across the sequence; what is left in a decoder layer is the per-token transformation that runs after attention. That block is the dense FFN of Section 1.1 — the same class, the same constructor signature DenseFFN(d_model, hidden), the same \(2 D H\) parameter count. Chapter 1 already counted what it costs; this section installs it inside the chapter-2 baseline and frames it as the replacement target. Every MoE variant the rest of the book builds is a drop-in substitute for this object.

Figure 2.4 — The skeleton that survives unchanged into Chapter 3. Today (top row) a single DenseFFN sits between a \((B, T, D) \to (B \cdot T, D)\) flatten and the inverse unflatten; tomorrow (bottom row) the same skeleton wraps a bank of expert FFNs with \(K\) chosen per token. The \((B, T, D)\) tensor on either end of the skeleton does not move. Rendered via TikZ in the PDF version.

today:   x (B,T,D)  ──flatten──►  (B·T, D)  ──► [ DenseFFN: W1 (D,H), W2 (H,D), GELU ] ──►  (B·T, D)  ──unflatten──►  y (B,T,D)

Ch.3:    x (B,T,D)  ──flatten──►  (B·T, D)  ──► [ Expert 1 ]                                  (B·T, D)  ──unflatten──►  y (B,T,D)
                                              │ [ Expert 2 ]  ◄── router picks K per token  ▲
                                              │     ...                                       │
                                              └─► [ Expert E ] ─────────────────────────────► ┘

         same skeleton; only the per-token transformation changes when MoE replaces DenseFFN.

Take the chapter-2 anchor mini-example: \(B = 2\), \(T = 8\), \(D = 16\). Pick \(H = 4 D = 64\), the standard expansion factor used throughout the book. The block stores \(2 D H = 2048\) parameters and spends \(2 D H = 2048\) multiply-adds per token, which is the cost we counted in Section 1.1 — nothing has changed except where the module lives. For the full \(B \cdot T = 16\) tokens of the anchor batch the dense FFN charges \(2 N D H = 32{,}768\) multiply-adds.

Name the new symbols. We keep \(B, T, D, H, N\) from Section 1.1. The only new objects here are the two helper functions: flatten_tokens(x) returns the \((B \cdot T, D)\) view of \(x\) along with the \((B, T)\) tuple needed to restore the shape, and unflatten_tokens(flat, (B, T)) is its inverse. We will use this pair literally unchanged when Chapter 6 vectorises dispatch.

Table 2.4 — What the dense FFN provides today and what each piece becomes when Chapter 3 replaces it with an MoE layer. Same shape, same per-token semantics; the only thing that changes is how the experts are selected.

Concept (today) Shape What it does Replacement in Chapter 3 \(x\) (input) \((B, T, D)\) Output of attention + residual; the decoder interface invariant from Chapter 1. Unchanged. \(W_1\) (up-projection) \((D, H)\) Single, shared up-projection for every token. Becomes \(E\) per-expert up-projections; each token uses \(K\) of them. \(W_2\) (down-projection) \((H, D)\) Single, shared down-projection for every token. Becomes \(E\) per-expert down-projections, weighted by router gates. flatten_tokens(x) \((B \cdot T, D)\) Row-major reshape; identity on the per-token view of the FFN. Section 6.1 uses this exact reshape as the dispatch unit. Per-token equivalence — \(\mathrm{DenseFFN}(x) = \mathrm{unflatten}(\mathrm{DenseFFN}(\mathrm{flatten}(x)))\). MoE preserves the equivalence per-token, but the function varies by token. Parameters (anchor) \(2DH = 2048\) \(D=16\), \(H=64\). Block totals (embed/attn/FFN): \(304 + 128 + 1024 + 2048 = 3504\). Bank: \(E \cdot 2 D H\) total; activated per token: still \(K \cdot 2 D H\). Diagnostic \((B, T, D) \to (B, T, D)\) Falsifiable: output shape equals input shape, AND \(\mathrm{DenseFFN}(x)\) is byte-identical to \(\mathrm{unflatten}(\mathrm{DenseFFN}(\mathrm{flatten}(x)))\). The same two checks survive into the MoE layer.

The block is one tensor equation written per-token.

\[ \mathrm{DenseFFN}(x)_{b,t} \;=\; \mathrm{GELU}\bigl(x_{b,t}\, W_1\bigr)\, W_2, \qquad W_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times H}, \;\; W_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times D}, \;\; x \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times D} \;\;\text{(per-token; no cross-token mixing)}. \]

The equation reads carefully: the subscript \((b, t)\) on the left and the right makes the per-token structure explicit. The right-hand side never indexes another row of the batch and never indexes another position in the sequence. Cross-token mixing is the job of attention; the FFN sub-layer is purely a token-wise non-linearity. That is the property the MoE replacement preserves — the per-token transformation can change from token to token, but the transformation is still per-token.

The listing re-exports DenseFFN from Chapter 1 (the constructor signature is locked by Section 1.6) and adds the flatten / unflatten pair.

# Re-export the locked-in Chapter-1 module. Same signature: DenseFFN(d_model, hidden).
from moe_from_scratch.ch01 import DenseFFN, dense_ffn_cost

def flatten_tokens(x):                            # (B, T, D) -> (B*T, D)
    B, T, D = x.shape
    return x.reshape(B * T, D), (B, T)

def unflatten_tokens(flat, bt):                   # (B*T, *) -> (B, T, *)
    B, T = bt
    return flat.reshape(B, T, flat.shape[-1])

# Mini-example: chapter-2 anchor (B=2, T=8, D=16) + H=64.
ffn       = DenseFFN(d_model=16, hidden=64)
y_direct  = ffn(x_mixed)                          # (2, 8, 16) from attention
flat, bt  = flatten_tokens(x_mixed)
y_via_flat = unflatten_tokens(ffn(flat), bt)

# Diagnostic (falsifiable):
assert y_direct.shape == (2, 8, 16)               # (B, T, D) interface holds
assert torch.equal(y_direct, y_via_flat)          # FFN is exactly per-token
assert sum(p.numel() for p in ffn.parameters()) == 2 * 16 * 64 == 2048

The example script under examples/ch02/ threads the seed-0 anchor batch through embed → attention → dense FFN, prints the parameter count, and verifies two things at once: the output shape is exactly \((B, T, D)\), and the FFN output is byte-identical whether the input is given as a \((B, T, D)\) tensor or as a flattened \((B \cdot T, D)\) tensor followed by an unflatten. That equality is the strongest possible test of "per-token" — any cross-token mixing inside the block, intentional or accidental, breaks it.

Run python examples/ch02/section_2_4_dense_ffn_replacement_target.py and verify the printed lines: D=16 H=64 T=8 B=2; embed, attn, and ffn all report shape \((2, 8, 16)\); params: 2*D*H = 2048 counted = 2048 MADs/token = 2048 total MADs = 32768; the byte-identical equivalence line prints; and the second configuration (\(D=32\), \(H=128\)) reports \(8192\) parameters with shape preserved.
